full_review:
Based on a Stephen King short story, "1408" (MGM/Dimension) delivers sufficient frights to count as a horror film and contains enough suspense pertaining to the afterlife to qualify as a supernatural thriller.

In other words, "1408" has the hallmarks of a classic ghost story, albeit an excessively discomfiting one, turbocharged by eye-popping special effects.

John Cusack portrays Mike Enslin, a writer who makes his living knocking out pulp guides on paranormal phenomena. His investigations into the occult have yet to shake his thoroughgoing skepticism about the existence of anything remotely otherworldly. We learn that his faith in God was destroyed by a tragedy involving his young daughter, Gracie (Jasmine Jessica Anthony).

Estranged from his wife, Lily (Mary McCormack), Mike is living in a Southern California beach community when an intriguing postcard arrives, beckoning him to an allegedly spooky chamber that could be ideal for his current book project, "Ten Nights in Haunted Hotel Rooms."

Room 1408 in Manhattan's Dolphin Hotel has a violent history that Mike can't resist. The numerals 1, 4, 0 and 8 add up to 13, after all.

The hostelry's reluctance to let him visit only piques his curiosity. In an ominous interview, manager Gerald Olin (Samuel L. Jackson) tries to dissuade him from checking in. Mike chalks it up to shrewd marketing but learns otherwise during a grueling overnight stay.

Swedish director Mikael Hafstrom assaults his audience's senses with a barrage of disorienting and genuinely terrifying scenes.

Cusack does a nice job of rendering the script's humorous shards, such as Mike's observation that charging $8 for nuts from the minibar is what's truly evil.

Unfortunately, the movie undercuts its credibility with too many twists.

And while forcing a character to confront his demons by scaring him into acknowledging a further dimension is standard procedure, the more outlandish and Byzantine the treatment, the less likely viewers are to be provoked into thinking on top of feeling.

So, too, the somewhat exploitative use of a child's suffering and maudlin concern for her fate, the excessive use of profanity, plus a trivialization of Mike's belief system in determining events may be issues for some Catholic viewers. We never find out whether Mike's ordeal has made him a believer again.

The film contains countless violent and morbid images and references, including many to suicide, frequent crude and profane language, and some sexual references. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
